title: Abba, Father (Galatians 4:1–7)
hook: no longer a slave but a child and heir
tomorrow: what does a wooden yoke have to do with being free?

segments.voice: Yesterday: all one, different and unranked, said to people who had been baptized. Which leaves an honest question about everybody else.

"We're all God's children." It's on mugs, in songs, at funerals. Then Paul writes that God sent his Son "That we might receive the adoption of sons." Adoption. Nobody adopts a child who's already theirs. It's exactly the kind of thing a kid asks at dinner, about a friend who doesn't go to church. So which is it: is every person a child of God, or is it a family you're brought into? Christians give two honest answers, and both come from the Bible. Here they are, side by side, each at its best.
screen: `WE'RE ALL GOD'S CHILDREN.` → `THE ADOPTION OF SONS.` → `WHICH IS IT?`

segments.voice: The first answer: every human being is God's child by being made. In Athens, Acts has Paul quote a Greek poet to a crowd who didn't share his faith: "For we are also his offspring." The prophet Malachi asks, "Have we not all one father? hath not one God created us?" On this reading, every face on the street is family before anyone believes anything. The second answer: in Galatians, child of God names a relationship that's received. Paul pictures an heir who, while small, "differeth nothing from a servant, though he be lord of all." Then God sends the Spirit "into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father." John's Gospel says the same shape: "to them gave he power to become the sons of God." Become. On this reading, everyone is made by God and loved, and adoption is the family name, given through Christ. Some readers hold both at once. Here's one to tell a friend: Abba is an Aramaic word, and Paul doesn't translate it away. He keeps it and sets the Greek for Father right beside it, the same pair Mark's Gospel puts on Jesus' lips in the garden the night before he died. Then Paul's conclusion, to each reader: "Wherefore thou art no more a servant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ."
screen: `WE ARE ALSO HIS OFFSPRING.` · `HAVE WE NOT ALL ONE FATHER?` · `ADOPTION: A NAME RECEIVED.` · `ABBA, FATHER.` · then, large: `NO LONGER A SLAVE.`

segments.voice: Say two words out loud, once, slowly. If you pray, let them be Paul's: Abba, Father. If you don't, say the name of someone who made you feel like family when you weren't, and let the sound sit in the room. Then stay quiet with it until the bell.
Adoption. Paul's word for being brought into God's family with a family name: no longer a servant, a child and an heir.
Pocket this one: no longer a slave, but a child who can say Abba. Until tomorrow.

chat.says: nia's making our flyers. she asked if she counts as a 'child of God' if she doesn't believe. help??
options: Christians say it two ways: made by God, so yes; and adoption, a family welcome. Both mean she's wanted.
No. Paul says only adopted children count, so she isn't one of God's children at all.
Yes, and it means she already believes deep down, whatever she says she thinks.
chat.meaning: Some Christians stress that everyone is God's offspring by creation; Paul's word adoption speaks of a family name received. Some readers hold both.

Abba.meaning: Aramaic for father, kept by Paul beside the Greek

Athens.meaning: the Greek city where Acts has Paul speak to a crowd

Malachi.meaning: a Hebrew prophet whose book is in the Bible

heir.meaning: the one who inherits a family's name and goods

notes: Written 2026-10-13 in the year-2-4 recipe (style pass and new-lesson data built in from the start).

v3 debate: two views inside Christianity on 'child of God': (1) every human being is God's child by creation (Acts 17:28–29, Malachi 2:10); (2) sonship is received by adoption through Christ (Galatians 4:5–7, John 1:12). The lesson says 'some readers hold both'. Confirm both are fairly stated and neither is presented as the settled view of all churches. Malachi 2:10 is addressed to Israel; the lesson uses it as one text people cite for the first view. Confirm the framing.

Abba: the voice says it is an Aramaic word (not stated in Galatians itself; standard lexicons agree). The myth item says 'some scholars warn daddy says too much' (e.g., James Barr's 'Abba isn't Daddy', 1988); confirm the hedge.
The KJV says 'servant'; the index carry says 'slave'. The lesson keeps both without a claim about the Greek word.
Paul writes 'sons'; the lesson does not add commentary on gender here (yesterday's lesson covered Galatians 3:28).
